Kernel developers have a reputation for being hard on newcomers. My experience was
the opposite. Over the [LFX Linux Kernel Bug Fixing Mentorship](https://wiki.linuxfoundation.org/lkmp)
with Shuah Khan, nine of my patches were applied upstream: eight in the Industrial I/O
(IIO) subsystem and one in the `sfc` network driver. None of them reached that state as I
first wrote them. Each was improved by someone on the mailing list: a maintainer, a
reviewer, or an automated test robot. This post is an account of that collaboration as
much as of the bugs themselves.

## Background: how a patch travels

The Linux kernel has no pull requests. A change is a plain-text email, sent with
`git send-email` to the maintainers and lists that `scripts/get_maintainer.pl` names
for the files it touches. Reviewers reply inline, and they show approval with tags such
as `Reviewed-by:` and `Acked-by:`. A subsystem maintainer then applies the patch to
their own tree. From there it flows into [linux-next](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/next/linux-next.git/),
then into Linus Torvalds' mainline tree during a merge window, and, if it is marked for
stable, into the [stable kernels](https://www.kernel.org/category/releases.html) people
already run.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-flow
%%| fig-cap: "The path every patch in this post followed. Preparing means building with W=1 and running checkpatch and kernel-doc; the review loop is where most of the work happened."
flowchart LR
    A[Prepare<br/>and check] --> B[Send to<br/>the list]
    B --> C{Review}
    C -- v2 --> C
    C -- tags --> D[Maintainer<br/>tree]
    D --> E[linux-next]
    E --> F[Mainline]
    D -. stable .-> G[Stable<br/>kernels]
```

IIO, maintained by Jonathan Cameron in [`iio.git`](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/jic23/iio.git/),
has two main branches. Fixes go to `fixes-togreg` and reach mainline in the current
release cycle. Everything else goes to `togreg`, through a `testing` branch, and waits
for the next merge window. This distinction matters later in the story.

## Learning the process the hard way

My first attempt, in June 2025, did not reach any maintainer: I sent it as an
attachment, only to my mentor. A second round, in June 2026, targeted the `sm750fb`
staging driver. I had based it on an old tree, so I was renaming variables that other
contributors had already renamed. The [kernel test robot](https://github.com/intel/lkp-tests) reported
build failures, and my duplicate resubmissions earned a polite request to stop.

These were useful failures. They set the method I used for every later patch:

1. Start from today's linux-next or the subsystem tree, never a stale checkout.
2. Build each changed object with `make W=1`, run `scripts/checkpatch.pl --strict`, and,
   for documentation, `scripts/kernel-doc -Wall` over the whole driver.
3. Search the list archives first. I kept local git mirrors of the
   [linux-iio](https://lore.kernel.org/linux-iio/) and
   [netdev](https://lore.kernel.org/netdev/) archives from lore.kernel.org, so I could
   check whether someone was already working on the same code.
4. Send each version once, with a changelog under the `---` line.

## Finding bugs worth fixing

Most of my search time went into static analysis: [Smatch](https://repo.or.cz/smatch.git),
[Coccinelle](https://coccinelle.gitlabpages.inria.fr/website/), `W=1` builds and
kernel-doc. Most of what these tools report is not a bug. I went through Smatch's 114
warnings on `net/` and about 20 in IIO. In every case I checked, the code was correct:
a signedness warning caused by a `__be16` enum, a pointer that a helper function
initialised where Smatch could not see it, and similar. Telling a false positive from a
real defect, and dropping it quickly, turned out to be one of the most important skills
of the mentorship.

Three real bugs came out of this search. Each of them also taught me something about
how C code can hide errors.

### Silent truncation in `scmi_sensors`

The kernel test robot had reported `do_div()` warnings in the
[SCMI](https://developer.arm.com/Architectures/System%20Control%20and%20Management%20Interface)
sensor driver, and Geert Uytterhoeven had noted on the list that most `do_div()` uses
in that driver were broken. Nobody had fixed them.

`do_div(n, base)` divides a 64-bit dividend by a *32-bit* divisor: `base` is stored in
a `uint32_t` on every architecture. The driver passed 64-bit divisors in seven calls.
One of them converts a sensor's update interval to a sampling frequency:

```c
static void convert_ns_to_freq(u64 interval_ns, u64 *hz, u64 *uhz)
{
	u64 rem, freq;

	freq = NSEC_PER_SEC;
	rem = do_div(freq, interval_ns);   /* interval_ns silently truncated to 32 bits */
	*hz = freq;
	*uhz = rem * 1000000UL;
	do_div(*uhz, interval_ns);
}
```

For any interval of 2³² ns (about 4.29 s) or longer, the divisor wraps around.
@fig-dodiv shows the result. The reported frequency is correct up to 4.29 s, then jumps
by orders of magnitude, and an interval that is an exact multiple of 2³² ns would divide
by zero.

![Sampling frequency reported by `convert_ns_to_freq()` as a function of the sensor
update interval. Before the fix, the divisor is reduced modulo 2³², so the result is
wrong past 4.29 s and diverges near every multiple of 2³² ns (dotted lines).](do_div.png){#fig-dodiv}

The fix replaces each call with `div64_u64()` or `div64_u64_rem()`, which take a 64-bit
divisor. The functions are not drop-in replacements, though. `do_div()` modifies its
first argument in place and *returns the remainder*, while `div64_u64()` *returns the
quotient*. I rewrote each call site separately so it kept its meaning:

```diff
-	freq = NSEC_PER_SEC;
-	rem = do_div(freq, interval_ns);
-	*hz = freq;
-	*uhz = rem * 1000000UL;
-	do_div(*uhz, interval_ns);
+	*hz = div64_u64_rem(HZ_PER_GHZ, interval_ns, &rem);
+	*uhz = div64_u64(rem * MICROHZ_PER_HZ, interval_ns);
```

Andy Shevchenko's review of v1 pointed out over-long lines, asked for the named unit
constants (`HZ_PER_GHZ`, `MICROHZ_PER_HZ`) instead of bare literals, and corrected the
format of my `Assisted-by:` tag. The v2 got his `Reviewed-by:`, and Jonathan applied it
to `fixes-togreg` with `Cc: stable`
([lore](https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261006045244.13993-1-kapoorarnav43@gmail.com/),
[commit](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/jic23/iio.git/commit/?id=850040f34265)).

### Three axes, one calibration value

The InvenSense MPU-9250 combines an accelerometer and gyroscope with an AK8963
magnetometer. Each magnetometer axis has its own factory sensitivity adjustment, called
ASAX, ASAY and ASAZ in the datasheet. The driver computes one scale per axis into
`magn_raw_to_gauss[]` and reads it back with `chan->address` as the index. But the
channel macro never set `.address`, so it was 0 on all three channels. The Y and Z axes
were scaled with the X axis's calibration, and had been since 2019.

I wanted to be certain before reporting this, so I inspected the compiled channel
tables with gdb rather than reasoning from the source alone:

| Channel | `.address` before | `.address` after | Calibration used before fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `in_magn_x` | 0 | 0 | ASAX (correct) |
| `in_magn_y` | 0 | 1 | ASAX (wrong) |
| `in_magn_z` | 0 | 2 | ASAX (wrong) |

: Magnetometer channel addresses read from the compiled object with gdb. {#tbl-magn}

The fix is a single line in the macro, `.address = (_chan2) - IIO_MOD_X`, which maps
X, Y and Z to 0, 1 and 2 in the same order `inv_magn_init()` fills the array
([lore](https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261011045619.357261-1-kapoorarnav43@gmail.com/),
[commit](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/jic23/iio.git/commit/?id=14265c34a218)).

### Positional initialisers and swapped startup times

While reading the same driver, I noticed a quieter problem. The hardware description
struct declares the startup times in one order:

```c
struct inv_mpu6050_hw {
	...
	struct {
		unsigned int accel;
		unsigned int gyro;
	} startup_time;
};
```

But every entry of the `hw_info[]` table filled them in the opposite order:

```diff
-	.startup_time = {INV_MPU6500_GYRO_STARTUP_TIME, INV_MPU6500_ACCEL_STARTUP_TIME},
+	.startup_time = {
+		.accel = INV_MPU6500_ACCEL_STARTUP_TIME,
+		.gyro = INV_MPU6500_GYRO_STARTUP_TIME,
+	},
```

C positional initialisers assign values by position, not by meaning, so the compiler
had no reason to complain. The accelerometer and gyroscope startup times had been
swapped for all 19 supported chips since 2021. Using designated initialisers fixes the
bug and makes the same mistake impossible to repeat.

Jean-Baptiste Maneyrol, the driver's maintainer at TDK InvenSense, acked both
`inv_mpu6050` fixes. Jonathan applied them to `fixes-togreg`, marked for stable
([lore](https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261011045710.357809-1-kapoorarnav43@gmail.com/),
[commit](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/jic23/iio.git/commit/?id=2b8d4cd20ac8)).

## Documentation, and why reviewers ask for more

The remaining patches fixed kernel-doc comments that no longer matched the code:
members that had been renamed or removed in `ad5686`, `inv_icm42600`, `inv_mpu6050`,
and `sfc`. These sound minor, but the review of these patches taught me the most
about how maintainers think.

When I sent a one-line fix for a stale `@vdd_supply` comment in `inv_icm42600`, Andy
gave it a `Reviewed-by:` and asked whether it was the only kernel-doc problem in the
driver. It was not. My v2 became a two-patch series that left the driver clean under
`kernel-doc -Wall`. From then on I checked the whole driver before sending any
documentation patch, and the `inv_mpu6050` patch fixed all 13 of its warnings at once.

On netdev, Simon Horman noticed that a member next to the ones I had fixed in `sfc`
was also undocumented. Looking closer, it was not used anywhere, so v2 removed it and two
other unused members. That patch got `Reviewed-by:` tags from Alex Austin at AMD and
from Simon, and Paolo Abeni applied it to `net-next`
([lore](https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261007175338.28683-1-kapoorarnav43@gmail.com/),
[commit](https://git.kernel.org/netdev/net-next/c/32a8010d2c30)). It was my first patch
applied anywhere in the kernel.

## Working with the maintainers

I was nervous before every early submission. The names on the `To:` line were names I
knew from `MAINTAINERS` files and commit logs, and every reply would be public and
archived. That nervousness faded as the replies came in, because they were generous and
precise.

Jonathan made me feel welcome from the start. When Jean-Baptiste called the startup-time fix "another good catch", Jonathan
replied "Absolutely" and applied it. He then suggested a follow-up, using named initialisers for the neighbouring `.temp` field, and added
"No problem if you have moved onto other things!" It was a small sentence, but it made
me feel like a contributor rather than a student.

He was also careful in ways that taught me about stewardship. On the `cros_ec_sensors`
patch he wrote that the driver "tends to be well maintained", so he would wait for its
own maintainers before applying it. Tzung-Bi Shih, a ChromeOS EC maintainer, reviewed it
the next morning, and Jonathan applied it that evening. When Joshua Crofts asked me for a `Fixes:`
tag on that patch, I traced the code back to the commit that introduced it and posted the
tag in the thread. Andy replied that there was no need to resend, because `b4` collects
tags from the whole thread. These are small things, but each of them is part of how
the community works.

The best moment was a run of emails late on 17 October. Within about twenty minutes,
"Applied to the togreg branch of iio.git" and "Applied to the fixes-togreg branch"
arrived for seven of my patches. I was thrilled. After the earlier failures, seeing them
applied one after another was the high point of the mentorship.

## A lesson in dependencies

The follow-up Jonathan suggested taught me one more thing. I based it on `fixes-togreg`,
because it edits lines that the startup-time fix had just changed. Joshua tried it on
the development branch and replied that it did not apply. The patch was fine, but its
context lines only exist where the startup-time fix exists. I explained this on the
list. The lesson is to always state a patch's base branch and dependencies below the
`---` line, especially when it builds on a fix that has not yet reached the development
branch.

## On using an AI assistant

I used an LLM-based assistant for analysis and to check my reasoning, and I disclosed
it with an `Assisted-by:` tag on each patch, as the kernel's
[policy on coding assistants](https://docs.kernel.org/process/coding-assistants.html)
requires. That policy is clear that responsibility stays with the human: I signed off,
built and tested every patch, and answered every review myself. The guidance on the tag's
format changed during the mentorship. Andy corrected my early format, and Jonathan later
dropped the tag from one patch because the guidance had changed again. It is a policy
still being worked out, and the community is working it out in public.

## For the next mentee

- Read [`submitting-patches.rst`](https://docs.kernel.org/process/submitting-patches.html)
  before your first patch, and the subsystem's maintainer notes, such as
  [`maintainer-netdev.rst`](https://docs.kernel.org/process/maintainer-netdev.html),
  before your first patch to that subsystem.
- Look for code that is wrong, not only code that warns. Tracing a bug to the commit that
  introduced it, with a `Fixes:` tag, makes a patch much more useful to maintainers.
- When a reviewer asks for more than you sent, they are usually right. Treat it as the
  start of a collaboration.
- Be patient. Maintainers batch their work, and my patches waited one to two weeks.
